When we see people attack empathy or say things like, “The fundamental weakness of Western civilization is empathy” (Elon Musk, 2025), we should ask ourselves, “What harm, pain, or hurt do they not want us to see or feel? Who do they want to hurt, humiliate, or dehumanize without accountability?

”Based on our research over the past 25 years, creating meaningful connections and human-centered systems requires a combination of compassion and cognitive empathy. I think of compassion as the daily practice and cognitive empathy as one its most powerful tools.

We define compassion as the daily practice of recognizing and accepting our shared humanity so that we treat ourselves and others with loving-kindness, and we take action in the face of suffering.

Most definitions of compassion share a commitment to action. It’s not just feeling, it’s doing. Compassion is fueled by accepting that we’re all made of strength and struggle—no one is immune to pain or suffering. Compassion is not a practice of “better than” or “I can fix you”—it’s a practice based in the beauty and pain of shared humanity.

Most researchers agree there are at least two elements to empathy: cognitive empathy and affective empathy. Cognitive empathy, sometimes called perspective taking, is the ability to recognize and understand another person’s emotions. Affective empathy, often called experience sharing, is one’s own emotional attunement with another person’s experience.

The empathy we desperately need is understanding what someone is feeling, not feeling it for them. If someone feels lonely, empathy doesn’t require us to feel lonely too, only to reach back into our own experience with loneliness so we can understand and connect. Affective empathy, feeling something along with the person who is struggling, is a slippery slope toward becoming too overwhelmed to offer meaningful support.

Again, empathy is a tool of compassion. We can respond empathically only if we are willing to be present to someone’s pain. If we’re not willing to do that, it’s not real empathy. And the lack of real empathy is 100% a major threat to civilizations.

Thank you to @toninovvva (on Instagram) for this powerful reminder.

You will NEVER win in business without the 3 R’s - Referrals, Recurring Revenue, and REVIEWS. 

1) Referrals 

Make it easy for people to tell their friends. 

Give excellent service, then ask if anyone else could benefit. Create a referral program, hold a contest, and do everything in your power to get your customers talking about you. 

Because do you know what your best customer has that you need? Friends who are more likely to give you business if they tell them about you. 

2) Recurring Revenue 

This isn’t me telling you to slap a subscription model over your tree-cutting business. At least, not exactly… 

Recurring rev is predictable revenue. It's much easier it is to project cashflow when you KNOW a certain amount revenue is already accounted for. Plus, your LTV will increase exponentially when you create a recurring revenue stream. 

Figure out how to sell packages that renew every month, quarter, or year. 

Sell packages, offer bulk discounts, and otherwise set up a system that makes it easy for someone to “set it and forget it.” 

3) Referrals 

I know its uncomfortable to ask but MAN is it important. 

Help people say nice things about you, by asking for a review post-purchase. Expect 1-5% of people to say, “dont ask me again,” and get used to rejection. 

I know most of you have never owned a business, but THIS is the core of what business owners need to do. People don’t blindly trust anymore, so they need to see others like them loving you. 

If you aren't already reaching out at least 1x a day to ask for a review from a happy customer, you will be amazed by the ROI.

For more than a decade, I lived the kind of life ambitious people are told to want. I helped build two companies past $1B in valuation and raised more than $300M in venture capital. By 33, I was Chief Revenue Officer at a venture-backed company, making more money than I’d ever imagined. And quietly falling apart.

I was burned out, anxious, drinking too much, and increasingly convinced that if I kept going, I might not see fifty.
Then one afternoon, in our house in Los Angeles, I had a panic attack so severe I ended up on the kitchen floor.

My wife, Jennifer, called 911. The paramedics came. And by the time they were standing in our home, it was impossible to keep pretending this was just stress.

When it passed, I knew that the life I was building wasn’t the one I wanted to live.

So Jennifer and I quit our high-paying jobs with almost no plan. We bought a house in the mountains of Upstate New York, drove across the country, and started our lives over.

In the years since, I’ve built a $15M one-person business with no employees and no investors, and an audience of 1.5M+ people has followed along. But that’s not the real story.

The real story is that I got my life back, slowly, unglamorously, one difficult choice at a time.

Today, I spend that life writing.

Every Saturday, I publish one essay about the choices that made it possible: leaving the obvious path, redefining ambition, using money for freedom instead of performance, and building something of your own without letting it consume you.

These are the choices that can look wrong from the outside and still be right for the life you actually want.

If that’s the kind of conversation you’ve been wanting to have with yourself, I’d love to have you with us.

My career got off to a really bad start.

I got fired 3x in a row for being "lazy."

6 years after the third firing, I was the CRO at one of the fastest-growing healthtech companies in the US.

After building that company to a valuation of over $1B, I quit and went all in on myself.

That silly little one-person business went on to create more than $15M in profit over 7 years.

When I look backward at the inflection points, a few things become crystal clear.

- I was healthy
- I was building skills
- I was bringing my best energy
- I was willing to take action before I felt ready

This is what I like to call the "Four-Part Edge" of leadership.

If you look at when I first started seeing some success, most of the focus was on energy and skills:

Work harder.
Learn faster.
Figure it out.
Make that call.
Take that meeting.

And that definitely worked. I wouldn't have succeeded without it.

But these days, I'm all in on the other side. The health and wellness part of the journey.

I want to wake up feeling good.
Drink coffee, do Wordle, and work out.
Take my wife out to an uninterrupted lunch.
Be someone people enjoy hanging out with.

And I still want enough ambition to chase ideas that scare me.

That’s the new combo I’m looking for.

Skilled.
Healthy.
Positive.
Action-oriented.

At 45, that feels way more powerful than just trying to outwork everyone around me.

My one-person business has been the catalyst for freedom and for creating my life around those four things.

If you want more control over your income, your time, and the way you spend your days, consider joining me.

I escaped the startup game with so many skills.

What I didn't have was attention.

So I started writing online in late 2018.

I started with the stuff I felt I knew best:

- Sales.
- Leadership.
- Building teams.
- Growing companies.

I kept showing up and sharing everything I had learned in the previous decade.

And slowly but surely, more people started paying attention.

That attention turned into:

- Consulting clients

- Digital course income
- Partnerships & sponsors
- Brand new business ideas

A useful skill is worth a little.

A useful skill that thousands of people know about can change your entire life in just a few years.

This is what I call creating your "Skill Signal."

Pick something you’re genuinely good at.

- Talk about it daily.
- Teach what you know.
- Share what you’re learning.
- Help people solve small problems.

Then? Just give it time.

You don’t need millions of followers.

My $900 AI lawnmower lost to a guy named Alon.

I was paying about $100 a month for lawn care. Then I found an AI-enabled, self-driving lawnmower on sale for $900. The thing paid for itself. Hit a button, cut my grass, perfect lawn forever. A little money upfront for a problem I'd never think about again. 

Hello Vibe Cutting!

I'm telling you this because it's what I'm seeing happen everywhere right now, including inside AppSumo. 

AI shows up with a promise you can genuinely believe. Then the real cost, the implementation, the maintenance, and what it actually delivers turn out to be somewhat else entirely. 

So it arrived and I told it to go cut. I figured. See you later, humans. No more need for you. 

Figured it would just look at my yard with its cameras and figure out the grass. Nope. First you have to map the lawn, supposedly can do it "automatically." The air quotes are for dramatic effect. 

The mower drove all over the place. Then it ran out of battery and crawled back to charge. I tried to map more and it mapped the wrong part of the yard. I tried again, finally got it to map the right thing.

It cut. Sort of. There were patches it missed entirely. It left the clippings exactly where they fell instead of bagging them. It didn't touch the edges. 

It did, however, find time to mow down a row of my wife's plants. She was not pleased. That was day one. Day two I learned it also has to sit in a specific spot to get GPS. Every problem I solved revealed the next one underneath it.

Here is the part that stuck with me. As amazing as the idea is, it's still only $100 to have a person do it, and do it better. Could the machine eventually beat that? Sure. Maybe.

My vibe cutting is the exact same gap I feel with vibe coding and AI right now. The promise is a button. Describe what you want, hit go, get a finished product. What you actually get is a thing that drives all over the place, runs out of battery halfway through and pisses off your wife. 

The demo is magic. The implementation, the cost, and what it actually delivers are still a long way from the pitch.

Will it get there? Maybe. Will it stay too expensive to be worth it? Also maybe. I don't know yet, and anyone who tells you they do is selling something.

What I do know is that Alon comes by twice a month, cuts the grass, blows the leaves, does a better job than my robot, and I like seeing him. For now the button I keep hitting is the one that calls Alon.

I returned the mower, I'll see Alon on Friday!
